text.tspan: An assistant that answers plain-English questions about supplier contracts,
backs every answer with the exact clause it came from, checks every figure
against that clause — and refuses when the documents don't say.
Group project (team of 2). I built the document and retrieval pipeline — sourcing, loading and cleaning, chunking, the
evaluation question set, vector and keyword search, fusion and re-ranking — then led integration and debugging, and built
versions 2 and 3, including the redesigned interface and figure checking. My teammate built the answer generation,
relevance gate, citation validator, API and first frontend.
Python · ChromaDB · BM25 · Sentence-Transformers · Groq · Gemini · SQLite · FastAPI · Streamlit
Built during a simulated industry sprint.

text.tspan: Procurement teams hold contracts with 100–200 suppliers, but the answer to a simple
question — what are our payment terms? — can be spread across a master agreement,
a statement of work, later amendments and price schedules. Checking one term by
hand takes about ten minutes: find the document, make sure no amendment changed
it, then find the exact clause. So people skip it — and invoices get overpaid, early-
payment discounts and renewal deadlines get missed, and expired supplier
certificates go unnoticed. A generic chatbot doesn't help: in a contract, a confident
wrong answer is worse than none.
Mostly real, public documents: 58 commercial contracts from the CUAD dataset
(Atticus Project), chosen for procurement relevance; 12 SEC EDGAR amendments
paired with their original agreements; and 18 public data-processing and service-level
agreements from vendors including Google Cloud, Amazon, Atlassian, Stripe, Twilio
and HubSpot. I added 70 synthetic price schedules and compliance certificates,
generated with a fixed seed, so every file type (PDF, HTML, Word, text) and clause
In total: 158 documents from 69 suppliers. Cleaning stripped headers, footers and
redaction marks and standardised dates, so each chunk keeps a stable ID that

text.tspan: Contracts are split at clause boundaries, not fixed lengths,
so every retrieved piece is a complete clause a citation can point to.
Meaning-based vector search finds paraphrases; keyword search
(BM25) finds exact terms like "Net 45" that embeddings can blur. The two ranked
lists are merged with Reciprocal Rank Fusion, then a cross-encoder re-ranks the top
Embeddings run on the machine instead of through an API. With
158 documents this costs nothing and keeps the free-tier model quota for
When an amendment is retrieved, the clause it
changes in the original agreement comes with it, and vice versa, up to three links
If the best match scores below a tuned relevance
threshold, the system refuses before calling the language model at all — no answer
is invented, and no quota is spent.
After an answer is written, code — not the model — confirms
that every citation exists in the documents and every number appears in the cited
clause. Passing answers get a "Checked" seal; anything else is marked for a person
When the two halves of the system first ran together, 3 of 223 tests failed and
generation didn't work at all. I led the integration and kept a debugging log of 37
findings — from installation failures and retired model names to answers refused after
an amendment upload — and fixed 24 of them. The rest are recorded as open, partly
fixed or by design. The log also records why the relevance threshold was re-tuned
three times as real questions exposed where it was too strict.
A labelled set of 67 questions: 30 drawn from real CUAD contracts (renewal,
termination, liability, pricing, compliance), 22 exact-value questions (unit prices,
payment terms, certificate expiry dates), and 15 questions the documents cannot
answer. The set was split into 40 tuning and 27 held-out questions. Measured on the
tuning set with real models and caching off: the correct clause was in the top 5 for 29
of 31 answerable questions, all 9 unanswerable questions were refused, and 1
Screenshot to add: the app answering "What are the payment terms?" for Orion
A checked answer: the payment period comes from Amendment 1, which replaced the original clause.
Every citation was found and every number matched the clause text.
93.5% recall@5, every unanswerable question refused, a 3.2% false-refusal rate, and
checked answers in one to five seconds. The final version has a redesigned interface
with per-contract conversations, a "Terms found" table showing which clause is in
force and since when, and an insights page tracking answer rate and speed against
